title: TypeScript Structural and Erased
subtitle: Shape compatibility, compile-time only, runtime validation

cards.front: Two facts that define TS's type system?
cards.meaning: It is structural (compatibility by shape, not by name) and erased (types exist at compile time only; runtime is plain JavaScript). That pair explains unnamed objects satisfying interfaces, why instanceof SomeInterface is impossible, and why Nest/zod validation is the runtime half of safety.

Two types are compatible when their members match — the needed shape is present — not because they share a declared name. Unrelated types with the same fields are often assignable (accidental structural match). High-level “duck typing”: if it has the properties you need, it fits.
OK when assigning an existing non-fresh variable — it structurally has x and y; extra z is fine. The object never had to be named Point.
cards.example: const obj = { x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }; logPoint(obj); // OK

cards.meaning: Excess property checks on a fresh object literal — a soundness aid on top of structural typing, not a switch to nominal typing. z is excess when the literal is passed directly where Point is expected.
cards.example: logPoint({ x: 1, y: 2, z: 3 }); // Error: z is excess on a fresh literal

cards.front: Why is extra z OK on obj but an error on a fresh literal?
cards.meaning: Variable obj already exists with its own inferred type; assigning it to Point only asks whether it has x and y. A fresh literal is checked more strictly for typos and unintended fields.
cards.notes: Structural typing plus a literal-specific guard.

cards.meaning: Structural (TS): compatible when the shape matches. Nominal (typical Java/C#): you need an explicit type relationship — extends, implements, or the same declared type. Same-shape unrelated types often assign in TS and not in Java/C#. TS interfaces are erased; typical nominal OO types are often reflective at runtime.
Yes, with private fields or branded/unique-symbol patterns when you need intentional distinction. Default answer: TS is structural.

Annotations, interfaces, type aliases, generic type parameters, and most type-only constructs are removed during emit. Output is JavaScript with no type metadata. Types guide the compiler; they do not execute.
cards.example:
function id<T>(x: T): T { return x; }
// emit: function id(x) { return x; }

cards.meaning: Impossible — interfaces and type aliases are not values. Trying value instanceof User is a compile error because User is not a value.
cards.example:
interface User { id: string; }
// value instanceof User // Error — User is not a value

cards.front: When does instanceof work in TS/JS?
cards.meaning: Classes leave a runtime constructor, so instanceof checks the prototype chain. Type aliases and interfaces emit nothing.
cards.example:
class User { constructor(public id: string) {} }
new User('1') instanceof User; // true at runtime

cards.meaning: Not always. Enums may emit runtime objects depending on const enum / preserve settings. Do not lump “all TS syntax vanishes equally.”
No runtime checks against generic T. It lies to the type system; runtime is just JSON.parse. Generics do not enforce shapes after JSON.parse or network I/O.
cards.example: function parse<T>(raw: string): T { return JSON.parse(raw); }

cards.meaning: A type annotation checks nothing at runtime — it is erased. Use JS checks the compiler can follow (typeof, instanceof on classes, 'prop' in obj, Array.isArray), a type predicate (x is User), or a schema library (zod / io-ts / Nest class-validator + DTOs). Validators are the runtime half of safety, not extra typing.

tsc type-checks and/or emits JS. Babel/SWC often only strip TS syntax — strip is not check. Common pipelines: tsc alone; tsc --noEmit plus a bundler; bundler-only (types can be wrong until CI runs tsc). “We use TypeScript” does not mean every build type-checks.

cards.front: Nest DI metadata — do interfaces survive erasure?
cards.meaning: No. emitDecoratorMetadata / reflect-metadata is extra emit around classes — constructor param types as runtime hints for the container. It is not interfaces surviving as runtime values.

cards.front: JS typeof vs TS typeof in type position?
cards.meaning: JS typeof checks runtime values (typeof x === 'string'). TypeScript's type-level typeof in type positions is a compile-time query of a value's type. Same keyword, different worlds.
